issue_context.title: Need benchmarks for iptables proxy golang performance hacks
issue_context.body:
A long time ago @wojtek-t did some optimizations to `pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go` around memory allocations (#46033, #46350).

Some of our refactorings since then have probably regressed this somewhat. OTOH, there have probably also been golang improvements since then that make some of the fiddly manual bits less necessary...

There are changes I would like to make that I have no idea of the performance impact of. eg:

```
@@ -1113,7 +1113,7 @@ func (proxier *Proxier) syncProxyRules() {
                                // in case we cross nodes.
                                proxier.natRules.Write(
                                        "-A", string(externalTrafficChain),
-                                       "-m", "comment", "--comment", fmt.Sprintf(`"masquerade traffic for %s external destinations"`, svcNameString),
+                                       utilproxy.Comment("masquerade traffic for %s external destinations", svcNameString)),
                                        "-j", string(KubeMarkMasqChain))
                        } else {
                                // If we are only using same-node endpoints, we can retain the
```

It would be good to have some sort of benchmark we could use to test changes against...

/sig network
/priority important-longterm

@danwinship et al

do you think it would be a good idea to build a simple interface for iptables that can self validate? something that would look like 

```
Rule.New(
WithChain(name),
WithComment(comment),
WithJump(chainName)
)

Rules.Add(rule)// <- this validates the rule logic
```

I toyed with something like this but did not follow-through.  I ended up writing an AST for iptables.  Maybe a more monolithic approach as a middle-ground?  Liek a big struct with all pre-allocated fields which we store in a free-pool and return them there for reuse?

I did manual micro-bench for `Write()` when we made it allow `string` or `[]string` and it was negligible.  We could check such a micro-benchmark in for posterity.

That said, I agree having a good signal of "did not increase allocations" or "perf is within norms" would be good for this.

There are performance test running periodically to detect regressions, and they also track kube-proxy memory usage

http://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-100Nodes-master&metriccategoryname=E2E&metricname=LoadResources&PodName=kube-proxy-e2e-big-minion-group%2Fkube-proxy&Resource=memory


In addition, scalability test jobs  dump the prometheus metrics , so you can explore the different metrics that run in the test, i.e. on a presubmit job with  100 nodes you can get the dump https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-jenkins/pr-logs/pull/109529/pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce-100-performance/1515984760160129024/artifacts/prometheus_snapshot.tar
and analyze the number of rules and the average time to sync, same for the golang memory metrics of kube-proxy, ....

![image (1)](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6450081/163795982-357d4d21-9c51-4c02-8ff4-3bc19c587c06.png)


![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6450081/163796032-ad5ec17a-e2de-44fc-aca9-833695661a60.png)


but those are very expensive and complicated to run, we should have something easier to run

@danwinship on further inspection, I found type assertion to be the reason for the increase in boost.

Current interface for writing rule
```
func (buf *LineBuffer) Write(args ...interface{})
```

I switched it to 
```
func (buf *LineBuffer) NewWrite(strArrays ...[]string) {
```

and with minor adjustment in write call
```
func pack(args ...string) []string {
	return args
}

rules.NewWrite(args,
    pack("-m", "addrtype", "--dst-type", "LOCAL",
    "--dport", strconv.Itoa(32320),
    "-j", "REJECT"))
```

@thockin @danwinship @aojea 

I tried minimizing the write calls to the buffer (on top of the optimization shared above in the thread) and got a performance boost of 50%, the readability is almost same but perf gain is significant.

If you guys think this is a good optimization I can start working on this.

```

```

Looking through iptables/proxier.go, it looks like we only use `[]string` in a few places now (all the refactoring got rid of most of the places where we used to have multiple rules using the same match clauses). So it would probably make more sense to switch to just `string` rather than just `[]string`...

> I tried minimizing the write calls to the buffer (on top of the optimization shared above in the thread) and got a performance boost of 50%

Most likely caused by doing fewer reallocations... if you add up the lengths of all of the strings and call `buf.b.Grow(n)` before you start writing it should have the same effect?

> If you guys think this is a good optimization I can start working on this.

So _this_ issue was more about "we need to have benchmarks in k/k so that we can measure the effect of future changes", _not_ "we should make things faster". Of course, making things faster is also good, but I feel like we should have the benchmarks first...

> "we need to have benchmarks in k/k so that we can measure the effect of future changes"

@danwinship benchmarks would depend on the environment and hardware from where they were produced. Are we looking for a benchmarking tool that computes [deltas](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat#:~:text=If%20we%20run%20%E2%80%9Cbenchstat%20old.txt%20new.txt%E2%80%9D%2C%20it%20will%20summarize%20the%20benchmarks%20and%20compare%20the%20before%20and%20after%20results%3A) between baseline (master) and optimization changes (feature-branch), where both the benchmarks would be computed in same environment.

> Are we looking for a benchmarking tool that computes deltas between baseline (master) and optimization changes (feature-branch), where both the benchmarks would be computed in same environment.

that's mostly what I had wanted, yes

review_comments:
We don't want to benchmark just a single random rule. We want to benchmark the rules _as the iptables proxier generates them_, so that we can test things like "if I make such-and-such change to how `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` services work, does that regress in performance?"

Even though the functions we're testing are in `utilproxy`, I think the benchmark will be in `pkg/proxy/iptables`, because that's mostly what we want to benchmark. We want (at least) a benchmark that is similar to `TestOverallIPTablesRulesWithMultipleServices`.
